question: In what city was the painter Odile Varenne-Mercat born?
document: Odile Varenne-Mercat (1891–1968) was a painter whose luminous river scenes earned her a modest but devoted following in both Canada and France. She trained first under the landscape painter Achille Duroc in Montreal, where she shared a cramped studio on Rue Saint-Denis with two other students, and later spent four years in Lyon copying the Old Masters in the Musée des Beaux-Arts. Her breakthrough came in 1924, when her canvas Fog over the Richelieu was shown at a salon in Paris and purchased by a private collector from Brussels. Throughout the 1930s she divided her time between a summer cottage near Kamouraska and a winter apartment in Quebec City, painting the St. Lawrence in every season. Critics often noted her restrained palette of greys, ochres and pale blues, and her habit of leaving small patches of bare canvas visible at the edges of her work. She never married, and her correspondence with her younger brother Lucien, a cartographer, remains the main source for scholars studying her methods. A retrospective organized in Trois-Rivières in 1972 brought together more than eighty of her paintings, and several of them now hang in regional galleries across Quebec.

question: What was the Polish runner Teodor Ralski's personal best time in the 1500 metres?
document: Teodor Ralski was a Polish middle-distance runner who competed during the late 1950s and 1960s and was known for his fierce finishing kick. Internationally, he won a bronze medal at the European Championships and reached the semi-finals at the Olympic Games, where a stumble on the final bend cost him a place in the final. Teammates remembered him as superstitious, always wearing the same faded red socks in competition. After retiring, Ralski worked as a physical education teacher and later coached junior athletes in Gdańsk, several of whom went on to represent Poland.

question: In what year did Hallam Pryce-Whitcombe patent his tidal regulator clock?
document: Hallam Pryce-Whitcombe was a Welsh clockmaker and engineer best remembered for his tidal regulator clock, an ingenious device that used the rise and fall of harbour water to keep its mainspring wound. He began an apprenticeship with a watchmaker in Swansea in 1871 and afterward worked for several years repairing marine chronometers for ships calling at Cardiff. The idea for the tidal clock reportedly came to him while he watched mooring ropes tighten and slacken against the quay. His first working model, built from salvaged brass and a cast-iron float, was installed on a pier at Tenby, where it ran for nearly three decades with only occasional cleaning. Pryce-Whitcombe secured a patent for the mechanism and later patented an improved ship's log and a lamp-trimming tool, none of which brought him much income. The clock drew wider notice when it was described in a London engineering journal in 1893, prompting visits from harbour authorities in Bristol and Liverpool. He married Gwenllian Hopkins in 1880, and the couple had five children. His workshop notebooks, filled with sketches of gears and floats, are now held by the National Library of Wales in Aberystwyth.

question: What was the title of the philologist Marisol Etxeberria-Lund's doctoral dissertation?
document: Marisol Etxeberria-Lund was a philologist whose work on the vanished Roncalese dialect of Basque helped preserve vocabulary that might otherwise have been lost entirely. Born to a Basque father and a Danish mother, she grew up speaking three languages at home and later studied comparative linguistics at the University of Copenhagen. During the 1960s she made repeated field trips to the Roncal Valley in Navarre, recording elderly speakers on a battery-powered tape machine she carried on muleback. Her doctoral research focused on verb morphology in Pyrenean dialects and was supervised by the phonologist Henrik Aagaard. She went on to publish two widely cited books, Voices from the Upper Valley in 1974 and The Grammar of Silence in 1981, the second of which examined how languages fade within families over three generations. Colleagues described her as meticulous to the point of obsession, often returning to a single village a dozen times to confirm one pronunciation. She taught for many years at the University of Bordeaux and supervised more than thirty graduate students. Her tape archive, comprising some four hundred hours of recordings, was digitized in the early 2000s and remains an essential resource for Basque dialectologists.

question: How tall is Bertrand Okafor-Hale's sculpture The Listening Ferryman?
document: Bertrand Okafor-Hale is a sculptor known for monumental figures cast in weathering steel and placed along rivers and coastlines. Raised in Liverpool by a Nigerian father and an English mother, he trained as a welder in the shipyards of Birkenhead before enrolling at art school in his late twenties. His early pieces were small bronze heads, but he soon moved on to large public commissions. The best known of these, The Listening Ferryman, stands on the bank of the River Mersey and depicts a cloaked figure leaning on an oar, one hand cupped to his ear. The work weighs roughly forty tonnes and took eighteen months to fabricate in a converted warehouse in Bootle. It was unveiled in 2009 before a crowd of several thousand people. Okafor-Hale's other commissions include Tide Keeper, a seven-metre figure on the Northumberland coast, and a cluster of three kneeling women in a park in Leeds. Critics have praised the way his rust-coloured surfaces change with the weather and the seasons. He has also taught sculpture workshops for young offenders, which he describes as the most important part of his practice.

Fantecchi depended heavily on the support of a wealthy patron, Count Ottavio Sanseverini, who financed the printing of his scores and lent him a villa near Bologna for the summer months. He married in 1902, and the couple's only daughter, Clelia, later became a respected piano teacher in Modena and spent much of her life cataloguing her father's manuscripts. Fantecchi's later works, including a string quartet and a setting of the Stabat Mater, were rarely performed in his lifetime. question: What company manufactured Ruth Ambersley-Cole's folding incubator?
document: Ruth Ambersley-Cole was an American nurse and inventor who designed a collapsible incubator for premature infants that could be carried by a single person and assembled in minutes. She trained at a nursing school in Baltimore and spent the early 1920s working in rural clinics in western Maryland, where she saw infants die for lack of warmth during long journeys to hospital. Her design used a folding wooden frame, a canvas cover lined with felt, and a pair of hot-water reservoirs that could hold their heat for several hours. She received a patent for the device in 1927 after two earlier applications were rejected. Ambersley-Cole spent several years trying to interest manufacturers, writing to firms in Philadelphia, Chicago and Boston, and eventually signed a licensing agreement with a medical supply company that produced the incubator in modest numbers through the 1930s. Her attorney, Franklin Dewes, later recalled that she insisted on a clause limiting the retail price. The incubator was used by visiting nurses across the Appalachian region and by the Red Cross during flood relief in 1937. In later life she taught obstetric nursing and wrote a short memoir about her years in the clinics.

question: How many variable stars did the astronomer Tomasz Wilczewski-Arn include in his catalogue?
document: Tomasz Wilczewski-Arn was an astronomer who devoted most of his career to monitoring variable stars from a small private observatory in the hills above Kraków. Trained in mathematics, he became fascinated by stellar brightness changes after reading the work of earlier German observers, and in 1912 he purchased a twenty-centimetre refracting telescope with money inherited from an uncle. Over the next three decades he recorded observations on more than four thousand nights, often working alone until dawn, and exposed roughly eleven thousand photographic plates. His great achievement was a catalogue of variable stars in the constellations of Cygnus and Lyra, published in three volumes between 1931 and 1938, which gave positions, periods and light curves for each object. The catalogue was praised for its precision and was used by observatories in Germany, Sweden and the United States. Wilczewski-Arn corresponded regularly with professional astronomers but never held a university post, preferring to support himself by tutoring. His observatory was damaged during the Second World War, and many of his plates were lost. The surviving notebooks were donated to the Jagiellonian University in 1951.

question: What was the name of Lieselotte Brandauer-Kies's first photography studio in Vienna?

During the week she carried a heavy plate camera through the city, photographing bakers, cobblers, bookbinders and umbrella makers at work. Her pictures were published in several illustrated magazines and gathered into a book, Hands of the City, in 1936. Two years later she emigrated to London, where she opened a second studio called Atelier Kies in Hampstead and photographed many fellow refugees. Her negatives from Vienna were stored with a friend and were rediscovered in an attic in the 1980s. Exhibitions of her work have since been held in Vienna, London and New York, and she is now regarded as an important chronicler of interwar urban life.

document: Elias Thornquist-Bayle was a Swedish railway engineer who designed a rotary snow-clearing attachment that kept northern rail lines open through some of the harshest winters on record. His interest in snow clearance grew from his early postings along the line to Storlien, where trains were sometimes stranded for days in drifts. In 1903 he produced drawings for a front-mounted rotary blade driven by a separate steam engine, and the first prototype was tested near Östersund during the winter of 1905. The design was refined over the next several years and eventually adopted on lines in Norway and Finland as well. Thornquist-Bayle also wrote a technical manual on locomotive maintenance in cold climates, which went through four editions. He married Ebba Lindqvist, a schoolteacher, and the couple raised three sons, one of whom became an architect. He retired from the railways in 1931 and spent his later years in a house overlooking Lake Storsjön, where he continued to sketch machines for his own amusement.
